passages.label: A
passages.text: In 1959, NASA employee James Modarelli designed the round red, white and blue insignia that later became known as the meatball. Its parts convey the agency's work without a long explanation. The blue sphere represents a planet, the stars represent space, the red wing stands for aeronautics and the orbit suggests space travel. These elements meet several criteria for a successful mark. They tell a story, connect the symbol to NASA's mission and create a distinctive image. The design is also evocative of an earlier age of space exploration because it appeared during NASA's first years. A viewer may not decode every element immediately, but the unusual combination can arouse curiosity about the agency behind it.

passages.label: B
passages.text: By the 1970s, however, the same detail that made the insignia expressive created a practical problem. NASA says that the meatball was difficult to reproduce and print with the technology of that period. Under the Federal Design Improvement Program, the firm Danne and Blackburn designed a cleaner logotype. Introduced in 1975, the red word NASA used strokes of one width and removed the crossbars from both letters A. The changes refined the agency's appearance for signs, documents and equipment. The decision was strategic because the new mark was simpler to reproduce and looked modern. Its curved connected letters soon earned it the nickname worm. President Reagan honoured the design in 1984 for being simple and innovative.

passages.label: C
passages.text: NASA retired the worm in 1992 and restored the meatball as its main identifier. That return did not erase the newer design from public memory. The worm remained on souvenirs and on images from the years when it was official. In 2020, NASA brought it back for a special role on the Demo-2 launch vehicle, which carried astronauts from the United States to the International Space Station. The agency explained that the retro design could help capture excitement about a new period of human spaceflight. Subsequent missions and products have also used it selectively. NASA nevertheless continues to retain the meatball as its primary symbol, so the return of one mark did not require the removal of the other.

passages.label: D
passages.text: NASA’s guidance illustrates an issue that arises after designers devise a symbol. A logo can be printed on fabric or used in mass production, and those settings can present a different obstacle from publication on a screen. A supplier may want to customise a product. One downside would be an image that was drastically changed to fit a small space. Product rules give suppliers a foundation for deciding what changes require permission. That can support innovation without making the identity hard for the audience to recognise.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A viewer may associate the round emblem with a space mission and the red lettering with a different period of design. The circular background can evoke a planet, whereas the connected letters resemble a single drawn line. Both can inspire designers to refine a mark around a small number of recognisable features. The practical criteria still depend on use. A shape that works on a large wall must convey the identity clearly when it is reduced to a small patch. Consistent use in recognisable settings can reinforce the link with the agency.

R_H2.passageTitle: How Five Rings Became a Global Symbol

passages.label: A
passages.text: In 1913, Pierre de Coubertin drew five interlocking rings in blue, yellow, black, green and red on a white background. He wanted an international emblem for the Olympic Movement after the 1912 Stockholm Games, where athletes came from all five continents. The design first appeared at the top of one of his letters, and it was presented officially at the Olympic Congress in Paris in 1914 and appeared at the Olympic Games in Antwerp in 1920. Those dates matter because they demonstrate that recognition developed as time goes on, and a simple sketch became a formal symbol through repeated public use rather than through one sudden advertising campaign.

passages.label: B
passages.text: People often associate one ring colour with one continent, but official Olympic material says this popular explanation is wrong. Coubertin linked the five rings together with the union of the five parts of the world. He chose the five ring colours plus the flag's white background because the six colours appeared in the national flags of the time. The interlaced form helps convey athletes meeting from around the world, and it does not provide a colour code for Europe, Asia, Africa, Oceania and the Americas. Correcting that myth is important because a logo's story should rest on historical evidence.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The rings also meet familiar design criteria. Their geometry is clear enough to recognise at a distance, and their arrangement is distinctive among international symbols, while they can evoke different ideas for different viewers. Some see the Olympic Games, others think of friendship, excellence or peaceful competition. Research commissioned by the International Olympic Committee after the Sochi 2014 Winter Games reported that 93 per cent of participants identified the rings correctly. Respondents across different groups connected them with ideas including global reach, diversity, peace and excellence, and the result made the rings the foremost symbol among the major global marks included in that survey.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Wide recognition creates both interest and a practical issue, and a host can devise a new identity and customise materials around it, while the central symbol provides a foundation. Large events use fabric and printed material in mass production. Because the available area is finite, a designer may face an obstacle when a large emblem has to fit a small ticket. Innovation in the surrounding design can help, and a downside of changing the basic mark drastically is that an audience may have to learn all over again what it represents.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Earlier and subsequent Games placed the rings in front of audiences through flags, stadiums and broadcasts. Each appearance helped reinforce the association with the Olympic Movement, and a small mark on a ticket may arouse as much curiosity about the design as a large display. Hosts can refine a surrounding image to suit their city and make strategic choices about where to place it. The shared symbol can still convey the same association if the design keeps the rings distinct. The shared design goes on to inspire new host graphics and can generate recognition even where no wording appears.

R_H3.passageTitle: When a Brand Name Leaves the Logo

passages.label: A
passages.text: Mastercard's visual history began with the Interbank Card Association, which received its formal charter in 1967 after bankers started building its network in 1966. A small letter i originally identified the organisation, and it remained in a corner when the Master Charge name appeared across two interlocking red and ochre circles in 1968. Master Charge became MasterCard in 1979, and the letter i disappeared the following year, and the overlapping circles survived these changes and became the distinctive visual feature against which subsequent redesigns could be judged.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Developments in reproduction and display shaped the redesigns that followed, and the 1990 version introduced 23 horizontal bars and italic lettering while retaining the overlapping circles, and the 1996 design used fewer bars, larger lettering and a shadow to improve visibility. Those adjustments responded to the needs of cards and printed displays, but a symbol also had to remain legible at different screen sizes. Mastercard therefore introduced a more streamlined identity in 2016, with two clean overlapping circles positioned above a lowercase wordmark, and the disappearance of the capital C was part of that typographic simplification. Viewers could recognise the red and yellow shapes despite the change in lettering and the removal of the striped pattern. The contrast matters because fine lines and lettering remain visible at some sizes but are harder to distinguish at others. A simpler outline can carry more of the design's identifying work when a display leaves less space for text.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The most strategic change came in January 2019, when Mastercard removed its name from the mark in selected uses. The company reported that more than 80 per cent of people could recognise the symbol without the word Mastercard, and that evidence supported a move that might otherwise have seemed risky. The two circles could now stand alone on cards, at physical and digital shops and in major sponsorships, and the change did not create a completely new picture or make the symbol resemble a rival. It used the most distinctive part of the existing identity, and the redesign therefore turned existing familiarity into evidence for change, and a mature brand can modernise while keeping enough familiar material to avoid confusion.

passages.label: D
passages.text: One downside of removing the text is possible backlash from people who associate it with the company. Designers can devise a test of recognition before they customise a product for a new context. Printing on fabric or preparing cards for mass production raises a separate issue, since a design may look drastically different at another scale. The old circles provide a foundation for innovation, and that can reduce the obstacle of asking every customer to learn a completely new sign.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Removing a name can generate curiosity and even suspicion if a new mark is unfamiliar, and the strategic question is whether viewers associate two distinctive circles with the company, or believe that the design happens to resemble another mark. Criteria for a useful test might include the ability to name the company without being shown the wordmark and to recognise it at typical sizes. An evocative colour combination may evoke recognition before the words do. The subsequent task is to refine the way the mark appears, retaining enough visual continuity to reinforce those associations and convey the same identity.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which statement compares what people saw in the earliest designs and after the simplification in 2016?
options: The small letter identifying the organisation was added back inside the circles in 2016.
Overlapping circles were already part of an earlier design, and the later version kept the shapes after changing the words and dropping the stripes.
The brand continued to use the first name, but the 2016 mark no longer had circles.
Before 2016 the brand used the same capital-letter wordmark with no changes.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why did smaller displays make the detail in the earlier designs a practical issue?
options: Visual recognition requires the number of lines to double whenever the size is reduced.
Words are always easiest to read in the smallest space.
Circles cannot be printed on either cards or screens.
People may struggle to see some lines or lettering when a design takes up less space.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which account correctly distinguishes the 2016 step from the 2019 step?
options: The earlier step simplified the sign while keeping a wordmark, and the later step used the circles alone in selected places.
The words were removed everywhere in the first step and restored in every context in the second.
The two events both replaced the original circles with the same unfamiliar drawing.
Only the later step considered a display and only the earlier one used circles.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why did viewer recognition make the removal decision less risky?
options: The people asked had all seen the name printed in each version they judged.
Removing text creates recognition automatically even if the image is unfamiliar.
Many people could already identify the company from the shapes without seeing the word.
The survey measured whether people liked the colour combination, not whether they knew the brand.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What makes earlier recognition helpful but insufficient to establish how the design will work in a new product?
options: An earlier survey guarantees the mark will appear identical on every material.
A recognisable shape can still print or appear differently on another material or at another size.
If viewers know the circles by name, printing equipment has no effect on the result.
The company needs a new set of colours every time the product changes.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What is a possible drawback of taking out the text?
options: Reproduction always becomes harder as the number of letters falls.
The two circles necessarily become a rival company's symbol.
The relative order of letters in the company name can no longer change.
Some people who link the words with the company may object.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What would be a useful test before using the circles by themselves at a new size?
options: Ask people to name the company from the image at the sizes they would actually see.
Tell people the company first and ask only whether they like red.
Use a mark larger than every display planned and check no other size.
Count how many letters remain without seeing if people recognise the design.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How did the long history of keeping the circles affect the choice to remove the word?
options: It forced designers to remove the circles before they could make the lettering smaller.
It meant research into what people recognised had no connection to later decisions.
A visual feature that survived earlier changes already signalled the brand for many viewers.
It established that the overall size must be identical on every card and screen.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A designer wants to restore the old striped overlap but leave the name off on very small cards. Which checks would follow from the article?
options: Add stripes of any width and check only whether the colours can be reproduced in a large poster.
Check if the lines stay visible at the new size and whether viewers can still name the correct brand without words.
Treat the older version's existence as evidence that the brand is always recognised without a name.
Test only after telling each person who owns the mark and how many bars there used to be.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion best fits the changes in the article?
options: Once a company changes its name, the shapes people knew must always be replaced.
A logo qualifies as modern only when designers remove all visual links to earlier uses.
Using text or not using it is a choice that can be made without considering audience or display.
A familiar shape can let designers simplify the mark, provided it remains recognisable in how people actually encounter it.
